title: A House for the Hymn
premise: Elodie Brightwater hosts a small-town overnight radio show, but lately the callers are people she buried last week—and they all hum the same hymn her grandmother forbade in the house. When photographs of the family farmhouse begin showing an extra chair at every table, Elodie realizes the thing that took her grandmother's voice fifteen years ago has been waiting for an heir. Returning to the house during harvest season, she must recover the hymn's suppressed final verse from the memories of the dead without singing it aloud, because singing it completes an invitation. In the end, Elodie chooses to sing the verse alone on air, binding the entity to herself and freeing the town—surviving, but forever with a second chair at her own table.
about_author: A. M. Kavanagh is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent a decade answering calls from insomniacs across three states and never quite stopped listening for the wrong voices. They live in a farmhouse they insist is ordinary, and they have never once sung along to a hymn.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. During her overnight show, a caller named Ruth asks for a song dedication; Elodie recognizes the voice of a woman whose funeral she attended Tuesday. The call ends in humming—a hymn Elodie knows from childhood. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional calm, the first crack in fifteen years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: The Chair That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Sorting her grandmother's estate photos for a memorial segment, Elodie notices every image of the farmhouse now includes an empty wooden chair no one remembers owning—one that appears closer to the camera in each successive decade. Her brother Marcus dismisses it as photo damage. Beat: the past quietly rearranging itself around her.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Another dead caller phones in, this time reciting the first two verses of the hymn before dissolving into static shaped like breathing. Elodie plays back the tape and hears a third voice underneath hers from a broadcast two nights ago—a voice she never spoke. Beat: horror turning inward; she is already compromised.

chapters.title: What Grandma Swallowed
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Skeptical but worried, Marcus visits the farmhouse to prep it for sale and finds the kitchen table set for three, though Elodie lives alone. He finds grandma's journal, its final pages torn out, and a burn scar on the doorframe shaped like a mouth. Beat: loyalty tested by evidence he can't ignore.

chapters.title: The Congregation of Last Week
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. She cross-references her dead callers: all died within seven days, all attended grandma's funeral, all were choir members in 1989—the year the church burned. Each call adds one line of the hymn. Beat: pattern recognition as terror; the song is being reassembled through her show.

chapters.title: Verse Three
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. A caller who drowned sings verse three flawlessly, then whispers 'don't learn the last one, girl.' Elodie researches the 1989 fire and finds the hymn was written locally—by someone whose name has been scratched out of every record. Beat: the town's complicity surfacing.

chapters.title: Houseguest
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Moving into the farmhouse temporarily, she wakes at 3 a.m. to hear the radio downstairs playing her own show, though it isn't broadcasting. On the kitchen table: the extra chair, pulled out, still warm. Beat: invasion of sanctuary; invisibility is over.

chapters.title: The Torn Pages
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Marcus confronts Elodie with the journal's missing pages and admits he found them years ago and hid them—to protect her, he says. She reads enough to learn grandma didn't forbid the hymn out of piety; she sang it, once, and something answered. Beat: betrayal braided with love.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon Countdown
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The local paper's archive reveals the hymn's composer hanged himself in the farmhouse attic in 1911, and every owner since has gone quiet or gone mad. The full moon is nine days out. Dead callers now sing in unison, harmonizing. Beat: clock started; stakes made cosmic and personal.

chapters.title: The Man Who Scratched His Name Out
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. A new caller—alive, elderly, former choir director—confesses on air that the congregation wrote the fourth verse together in 1989 as a bargain: their voices in exchange for the town's prosperity. The fire wasn't an accident; it was a payment. Beat: collective guilt; power's corruption made literal.

chapters.title: Static Communion
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Attempting to silence the phenomenon, Elodie pre-records the whole week's shows. The station airs them anyway—with additions: her voice saying things she never said, inviting listeners to the farmhouse. Beat: loss of control over her own instrument, her identity hijacked.

chapters.title: Marcus Sings
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Alone at the farmhouse, Marcus hums the melody absently while working—and the house answers, walls swelling like lungs. He stops mid-note but the entity keeps his hum, replaying it. He hides this from Elodie. Beat: the price of survival begins accruing interest; guilt and secrecy deepen.

chapters.title: The Choir Assembles
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The dead begin arriving—not calling, arriving—standing at the property line each dusk, mouths moving in silence. Among them, grandma, who only points at the attic. Beat: grief weaponized; the dead aren't malicious, they're conscripted.

chapters.title: Attic Hymnal
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. In the attic she finds the composer's hand-bound hymnal, the final verse inked over so heavily the page is punctured. Under lamplight, the scratched-out name resolves: Brightwater. Her family wrote the song. Beat: inheritance horror; the curse is a birthright.

chapters.title: Verse Four, Almost
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Deciphering the obscured verse through candle-shadows and the dead choir's silent mouthing, Elodie gets most of it—but the last line refuses to be read; eyes slide off it. The moon is four days out. Beat: tantalizing near-knowledge; frustration sharpened into obsession.

chapters.title: What Marcus Gave
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. The entity collects on Marcus's hum: his reflection starts singing without him, and he begins losing words—he says 'kettle' and means 'sister.' He finally confesses everything to Elodie. Beat: sacrifice foreshadowed; loyalty choosing truth at last, too late to be free.

chapters.title: The Director's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The ex-choir director offers her an out: give him the show, let him sing the verse, take the burden. But Elodie sees what fifteen years of his bargain cost him—he hasn't aged since 1989 and can't remember his daughter's face. Beat: temptation refused; survival at any price exposed as its own death.

chapters.title: Night Before Harvest
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The dead choir crosses the property line at moonrise-minus-one and fills the farmhouse, singing verses one through three in perfect harmony, waiting for a fourth voice. Grandma's ghost presses the hymnal into Elodie's hands and, for the first time, speaks: 'Finish it better than we did.' Beat: terrible benediction; the mantle accepted.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. At dawn before the full moon, reading by the light of burning curtains, Elodie finally perceives the hidden line—it isn't an invitation; it's a binding, a song meant to cage the thing the congregation fed. The composer didn't die of guilt; he died holding the lock shut. Beat: revelation reframing everything; hope with teeth.

chapters.title: On Air, Alone
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Climax. Under the harvest moon, Elodie broadcasts from the farmhouse itself and sings all four verses solo, refusing harmony, refusing accompaniment, taking the covenant entire. The house screams, the extra chair splinters, the dead choir bows and releases. The entity pours into the open channel—into her. Beat: white-hot sacrifice; power seized rather than suffered.

chapters.title: After the Song
chapters.summary: POV Marcus. Weeks later, the show runs again, quieter. Callers are living. But Marcus watches his sister pause mid-sentence sometimes, listening to something just off-frequency, and her shadow occasionally sits down before she does. Beat: bittersweet aftermath; victory with a resident tenant.

chapters.title: A House for the Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Final chapter. Elodie sets her own table for two, then—after a moment—adds a third chair. She signs off her show with a new ritual: 'This is Elodie Brightwater, and tonight, I'm doing the singing.' The last line of the hymn hums faintly under her sign-off, held, not spoken. Beat: coexistence; the price of survival paid in perpetuity, owned with open eyes.
